claim: Tetraploidy has a documented role in tumorigenesis.
source: Tetraploidy has long been of interest to both cell and cancer biologists, partly because of its documented role in tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to existing literature about tetraploidy's role in tumorigenesis.

claim: Tetraploid cells evolved in culture lack extra centrosomes.
source: However, tetraploid cells evolved in culture have been shown to lack extra centrosomes.
evidence: The claim references previous observations from the literature.

claim: Populations of newly formed tetraploid cells rapidly evolve in vitro to retain a near-tetraploid chromosome number while losing the extra centrosomes gained at the time of tetraploidization.
source: Here, using a combination of fixed cell analysis, live cell imaging, and mathematical modeling, we show that populations of newly formed tetraploid cells rapidly evolve in vitro to retain a near-tetraploid chromosome number while losing the extra centrosomes gained at the time of tetraploidization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fixed cell analysis, live cell imaging, and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Centrosome loss in tetraploid cells happens through a process of natural selection in which tetraploid cells that inherit a single centrosome during a bipolar division with asymmetric centrosome clustering are favored for long-term survival.
source: This appears to happen through a process of natural selection in which tetraploid cells that inherit a single centrosome during a bipolar division with asymmetric centrosome clustering are favored for long-term survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many species across the tree of life are thought to have had polyploid ancestors at some point in their evolutionary history.
source: Organismal polyploidy is confined to certain taxa, but many species across the tree of life are thought to have had polyploid ancestors at some point in their evolutionary history (Comai, 2005; Smith and Keinath, 2015; Smith et al., 2013; Wolfe, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Polyploidy is thought to contribute to speciation and evolution.
source: and polyploidy is thought to contribute to speciation and evolution (Bennett, 2004; Otto and Whitton, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In vertebrates, organismal polyploidy is rare.
source: In vertebrates, organismal polyploidy is rare
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Among mammals, organismal polyploidy has only been described in a single species.
source: and among mammals it has only been described in a single species (Gallardo et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Within individual diploid mammals, some tissues physiologically develop to have a higher ploidy than the majority of somatic cells.
source: However, within individual diploid mammals, some tissues physiologically develop to have a higher ploidy than the majority of somatic cells (Nagl, 1990; Orr-Weaver, 2015; Øvrebø and Edgar, 2018; Schoenfelder and Fox, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Polyploidy is linked with cancer pathology.
source: Polyploidy can also occur outside of the context of normal development, and is linked with both pathology (particularly cancer [Ganem et al., 2007]) and aging (Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Polyploidy is linked with aging.
source: Polyploidy can also occur outside of the context of normal development, and is linked with both pathology (particularly cancer [Ganem et al., 2007]) and aging (Tanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Tetraploid cells are commonly found in premalignant lesions and tumors at different stages.
source: Tetraploid cells are commonly found in premalignant lesions and tumors at different stages (Davoli and de Lange, 2011; Galipeau et al., 1996; Olaharski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Close to 40% of all cancers had a tetraploid intermediate stage at some point during tumor evolution.
source: Furthermore, meta-analysis of catalogued tumor genomes has provided evidence that close to 40% of all cancers – even those that were not tetraploid at the time of sampling – had a tetraploid intermediate stage at some point during tumor evolution (Zack et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis study.

claim: Several studies have shown a direct, causative link between tetraploidy and tumorigenesis.
source: Consistent with this, several studies have shown a direct, causative link between tetraploidy and tumorigenesis (Fujiwara et al., 2005; Nguyen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In proliferating cells, tetraploidy can arise via cytokinesis failure, cell fusion, endoreduplication, and mitotic slippage.
source: In proliferating cells, tetraploidy can arise via abnormal cell cycle events, including cytokinesis failure, cell fusion, endoreduplication, and mitotic slippage (Davoli and de Lange, 2011; Dikovskaya et al., 2007; Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Larsson et al., 2008; Rieder, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most tetraploidization events result in the concomitant acquisition of extra centrosomes along with genome duplication.
source: Most of these events result in the concomitant acquisition of extra centrosomes along with genome duplication.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about tetraploidization mechanisms.

claim: Both tetraploidy and extra centrosomes have been shown to trigger a p53-dependent arrest in some experimental systems.
source: Importantly, both tetraploidy and extra centrosomes have been shown to trigger a p53-dependent arrest in some experimental systems (Andreassen et al., 2001; Fava et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes have been shown to promote chromosomal instability.
source: In experimental systems in which such an arrest does not occur, extra centrosomes have been shown to promote chromosomal instability (Ganem et al., 2009; Silkworth et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes promote invasive/migratory behavior.
source: and invasive/migratory behavior (Godinho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes promote and in some cases are sufficient to drive tumorigenesis in vivo.
source: Recent studies have also shown that extra centrosomes promote and in some cases are sufficient to drive tumorigenesis in vivo (Levine et al., 2017; Serçin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It has been speculated that the extra centrosomes emerging as a result of tetraploidization may drive chromosomal instability and, in turn, tumorigenesis.
source: Based on these studies, it has been speculated that the extra centrosomes emerging as a result of tetraploidization may drive chromosomal instability and, in turn, tumorigenesis (Storchova and Pellman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature presenting a hypothesis.

claim: Cytokinesis failure does not result in stable centrosome amplification in a cell population.
source: However, it was previously reported that cytokinesis failure does not result in stable centrosome amplification in a cell population (Krzywicka-Racka and Sluder, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Clones of tetraploid or near-tetraploid cells displayed normal centrosome numbers.
source: Moreover, anecdotal reports (Ganem et al., 2009; Godinho et al., 2014; Kuznetsova et al., 2015; Potapova et al., 2016) have indicated that clones of tetraploid or near-tetraploid cells displayed normal centrosome numbers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multipolar divisions were frequent in newly formed tetraploid DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells.
source: We found that multipolar divisions were frequent in both cell types (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Spindle poles in multipolar ana-/telophase cells always contained centrosomes.
source: This fixed-cell analysis and analysis of live RPE-1 p53-/- cells with GFP-tagged centrin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D) also confirmed that spindle poles always contained centrosomes (i.e., two centrin dots), as acentrosomal poles were never observed in multipolar ana-/telophase cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fixed-cell analysis and live cell imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: All live binucleate cells observed contained supernumerary centrosomes.
source: Furthermore, all of the live binucleate cells that we observed contained supernumerary centrosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Centrosomes in binucleate cells were duplicated prior to mitosis and were never lost/extruded during mitosis.
source: These centrosomes were duplicated prior to mitosis and were never lost/extruded during mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Only ~20–30% of newly formed tetraploid cells underwent bipolar anaphase.
source: The observation that only ~20–30% of newly formed tetraploid cells underwent bipolar anaphase indicates that centrosome clustering is not prevalent in newly formed tetraploid cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tripolar or tetrapolar anaphases did not always generate three or four daughter cells, respectively.
source: However, when we followed these multipolar mitoses through cytokinesis, we found that tripolar or tetrapolar anaphases did not always generate three or four daughter cells, respectively (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The DNA corresponding to two or more anaphase poles was often enclosed in a single daughter cell in multipolar divisions.
source: Instead, the DNA corresponding to two or more anaphase poles was often enclosed in a single daughter cell, giving rise to binucleated or, rarely, trinucleated daughter cells (Figure 1D–F), consistent with previous observations (Chen et al., 2016; Wheatley and Wang, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F and citations to previous observations.

claim: Immediately after DCB washout, approximately 80% of the DLD-1 population and 60% of the RPE-1 p53-/- population were tetraploid.
source: Immediately after drug washout, we observed a tetraploid fraction corresponding to approximately 80% and 60% of the population for DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells, respectively (Figure 2C–E,G, day 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E,G.

claim: Two days after DCB washout, high frequencies of cells with chromosome counts in the hypotetraploid/hyperdiploid range were observed.
source: Two days after DCB washout, we observed high frequencies of cells with chromosome counts in the hypotetraploid/hyperdiploid range (Figure 2B, middle panel; Figure 2C–E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C-E, and 2G.

claim: Chromosome distribution to daughter cells was balanced in bipolar divisions.
source: Indeed, by quantifying DNA fluorescence of separated chromosome masses in fixed ana-/telophase cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), we observed that while chromosome distribution to the daughter cells was balanced in bipolar divisions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Chromosome distribution greatly deviated from an equal distribution in multipolar mitoses.
source: it greatly deviated from an equal distribution in multipolar mitoses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D), indicating that the daughter cells in multipolar divisions inherit variable proportions of the genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The fraction of cells with highly abnormal chromosome numbers rapidly decreased over the course of the 12 day experiment in both cell types.
source: However, the fraction of cells with highly abnormal chromosome numbers rapidly decreased over the course of the 12 day experiment in both cell types and highly aneuploid cells were virtually eliminated from the DLD-1 population by day 12, leaving sub-populations of near-diploid cells (presumably derived from cells that did not respond to the initial DCB treatment) and near-tetraploid cells (Figure 2B,C–E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C-E, and 2G.

claim: The appearance and disappearance of highly aneuploid cells corresponded to an increase followed by a decline in the fraction of dead cells between day 2 and 6 in both cell types.
source: Indeed, the appearance and disappearance of highly aneuploid cells corresponded to an increase followed by a decline in the fraction of dead cells between day 2 and 6 in both cell types (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2H.

claim: Cell death rates were lower in RPE-1 p53-/- compared to DLD-1 cells.
source: However, cell death rates were lower in RPE-1 p53-/- compared to DLD-1 cells (Figure 2F vs. Figure 2H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and 2H.

claim: Daughter nuclei emerging from multipolar divisions in tetraploid cells were very likely to bear a monosomy or nullisomy for at least one chromosome.
source: The model predicted that daughter nuclei emerging from multipolar divisions in tetraploid cells were very likely to bear a monosomy or nullisomy for at least one chromosome (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by predictions from a probabilistic model shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Daughter cells produced by multipolar divisions were more likely to die or arrest compared to cells produced by bipolar divisions.
source: This was confirmed in long-term time lapse microscopy experiments in newly formed tetraploid DLD-1 cells (Figure 3D), which showed that daughter cells produced by multipolar divisions were more likely to die or arrest compared to cells produced by bipolar divisions (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from long-term time lapse microscopy shown in Figure 3D, 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diploid and near-triploid cells undergoing multipolar divisions produce daughter cells that arrest or die.
source: Previous studies have shown that diploid and near-triploid cells undergoing multipolar divisions produce daughter cells that arrest or die (Ganem et al., 2009; Gisselsson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tetraploid cells undergoing multipolar divisions produce daughter cells that arrest or die.
source: Our data indicate that this is also the case for tetraploid cells undergoing multipolar divisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of the G1 cell population containing supernumerary centrioles after a 20 hr cytokinesis block was 90% in DLD-1 cells and 87.3% in RPE-1 p53-/- cells.
source: the fraction of the G1 cell population containing supernumerary centrioles after a 20 hr cytokinesis block was 90% and 87.3% in DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of cells with supernumerary centrioles rapidly diminished over the 12 day observation period, reaching frequencies close to the frequencies in the parental populations.
source: However, this fraction rapidly diminished over the 12 day observation period, reaching frequencies that are close to the frequencies of cells with supernumerary centrioles in the parental populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of cells with supernumerary centrioles at day 12 was substantially smaller than the fraction of cells with ~4N chromosome number.
source: Moreover, the fraction of cells with supernumerary centrioles at day 12 (Figure 4C–D) was substantially smaller than the fraction of cells with ~4N chromosome number (16.3% and 13.3% vs. 63% and 33%, respectively, in DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/-; compare 'Day 12' data from Figure 4C,D and Figure 2E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 2E,G.

claim: A large fraction of the tetraploid cells that are present 12 days post-cytokinesis failure have lost their extra centrosomes.
source: Indeed, statistical analysis showed a highly significant difference between the number of cells with ~4N chromosome number and cells with extra centrosomes at day 12 for both DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells (two-sided Chi square test, p<0.0001 for both cell lines), indicating that a large fraction of the tetraploid cells that are present 12 days post-cytokinesis failure have lost their extra centrosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Nearly equal numbers of bipolar DLD-1 cells with symmetric vs. asymmetric centrosome clustering were found in late mitosis.
source: We found nearly equal numbers of bipolar DLD-1 cells with symmetric vs. asymmetric centrosome clustering in late mitosis (metaphase, anaphase, or telophase)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fixed cell analysis.

claim: Bipolar RPE-1 p53-/- cells showed a slight bias towards symmetric clustering of centrosomes.
source: while bipolar RPE-1 p53-/- showed a slight bias towards symmetric clustering of centrosomes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Model I predicted centrosome loss over a much shorter time scale than was observed experimentally for either DLD-1 or RPE-1 p53-/- cells.
source: Although this model (Model I) captured centrosome loss, it predicted centrosome loss over a much shorter time scale than was observed experimentally for either DLD-1 or RPE-1 p53-/- cells (Figure 5D–E, orange line).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The final fraction of cells with extra centrosomes predicted from Model I was substantially lower than what was experimentally observed.
source: The final fraction of cells with extra centrosomes predicted from the model was also substantially lower than what was experimentally observed (Figure 5D–E, orange line).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: When SC cells were included in Model II, the model output was no longer constrained by the probability of cytokinesis failure.
source: When such SC cells were included in the model (Model II, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), the model output was no longer constrained by the probability of cytokinesis failure (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and 3B.

claim: The final fraction of cells with extra centrosomes in Model II could match the experimentally observed values.
source: and the final fraction of cells with extra centrosomes could match the experimentally observed values (Figure 5D–E, blue line).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Asymmetric centrosome clustering, along with a selective advantage of cells that inherit a single centrosome, is sufficient to explain the loss of extra centrosomes in newly formed tetraploid cells.
source: Altogether, our modeling results show that asymmetric centrosome clustering, along with a selective advantage of cells that inherit a single centrosome, is sufficient to explain the loss of extra centrosomes in newly formed tetraploid cells, leading to the evolution of cell populations with tetraploid chromosome numbers but normal centrosome numbers (i.e., 1 centrosome, 2 centrioles in G1 tetraploid cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells that divided in a bipolar manner showed a mix of symmetric and asymmetric centrosome clustering without a strong preference for one mode.
source: We found that cells that divided in a bipolar manner showed a mix of symmetric and asymmetric centrosome clustering without a strong preference for one mode (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with our fixed-cell data (Figure 5A–C; two-sided Fisher's exact test, p=0.8224 and p=0.2243 for fixed vs. live cell data in DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/-, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison with fixed-cell data in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Cells that inherited a normal centrosome number were significantly more likely than cells that inherited supernumerary centrosomes to divide in a bipolar manner in both DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells.
source: Cells that inherited a normal centrosome number (1 centrosome/2 centrioles) were significantly more likely than cells that inherited supernumerary centrosomes to divide in a bipolar manner in both DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Cells that inherited too many centrosomes went through a mix of fates, dominated by multipolar divisions, arrest, and cell death.
source: In contrast, cells that inherited too many centrosomes went through a mix of fates, dominated by multipolar divisions, arrest, and cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Populations of stably dividing tetraploid cells containing a normal number of centrosomes can arise via asymmetric clustering of centrosomes (3:1) in bipolar mitoses and selective pressure against cells that inherit extra centrosomes.
source: These data, together with our mathematical modeling, strongly suggest that populations of stably dividing tetraploid cells containing a normal number of centrosomes can arise via asymmetric clustering of centrosomes (3:1) in bipolar mitoses and selective pressure against cells that inherit extra centrosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 90% of cells with extra centrioles displayed a bipolar configuration at day 12 compared with just 28% in newly formed tetraploid cells at Day 0.
source: As predicted by our model, we found that approximately 90% of cells with extra centrioles displayed a bipolar configuration at day 12 compared with just 28% in newly formed tetraploid cells at Day 0 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fixed cell analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When extra centrosomes arise, they may only be retained when cells can cluster them efficiently, whereas cells that cannot cluster their centrosomes efficiently may disappear from the population.
source: These results suggest that when extra centrosomes arise, they may only be retained when cells can cluster them efficiently, whereas cells that cannot cluster their centrosomes efficiently may disappear from the population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and modeling results.

claim: Populations of newly formed tetraploid cells rapidly evolve in vitro to retain a near-tetraploid chromosome number while losing the extra centrosomes gained at the time of tetraploidization in two different cell lines.
source: Here, we show, in two different cell lines, that populations of newly formed tetraploid cells rapidly evolve in vitro to retain a near-tetraploid chromosome number while losing the extra centrosomes gained at the time of tetraploidization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tetraploid cells that inherit a single centrosome during a bipolar division with asymmetric centrosome clustering are favored for long-term survival.
source: Specifically, tetraploid cells that inherit a single centrosome during a bipolar division with asymmetric centrosome clustering are favored for long-term survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The majority of cells with extra centrosomes are eventually eliminated because of their high probability of undergoing multipolar division.
source: Conversely, the majority of cells with extra centrosomes are eventually eliminated because of their high probability of undergoing multipolar division, which has a high likelihood of producing daughters with insufficient amounts of genetic material (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The pattern of centrosome number evolution after tetraploidization is common to both cancer (DLD-1) and non-cancer (RPE-1) cells.
source: Our study also shows that this pattern of centrosome number evolution after tetraploidization is common to both cancer (DLD-1) and non-cancer (RPE-1) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both DLD-1 and RPE-1 p53-/- cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tetraploidization occurs at some point during the progression of a large fraction of tumors.
source: Cancer genome sequencing data indicated that tetraploidization occurs at some point during the progression of a large fraction of tumors (Zack et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to cancer genome sequencing data.

claim: Tetraploid mouse epithelial cells were shown to be more tumorigenic than their non-tetraploid counterparts when injected in nude mice.
source: Moreover, tetraploid mouse epithelial cells were shown to be more tumorigenic than their non-tetraploid counterparts when injected in nude mice (Fujiwara et al., 2005; Nguyen et al., 2009; Davoli and de Lange, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Centrosome amplification is frequently observed in the pre-malignant stages of certain cancers.
source: This idea is supported by the following observations: centrosome amplification is frequently observed in the pre-malignant stages of certain cancers (Chan, 2011; Lopes et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Centrosome amplification is observed in a large fraction of human tumors.
source: and is observed in a large fraction of human tumors (D'Assoro et al., 2002; Gustafson et al., 2000; Lingle et al., 1998; Pihan et al., 1998; Sato et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Centrosome amplification correlates with poor prognosis/advanced disease stage in human tumors.
source: in which it correlates with poor prognosis/advanced disease stage (Lopes et al., 2018; Godinho and Pellman, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes can promote tumorigenesis in mouse.
source: extra centrosomes can promote tumorigenesis in mouse (Levine et al., 2017; Serçin et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes enhance the invasive behavior of mammary epithelial cells grown in 3D cultures.
source: and enhance the invasive behavior of mammary epithelial cells grown in 3D cultures (Godinho et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Supernumerary centrosomes promote chromosome mis-attachment and mis-segregation, leading to chromosomal instability.
source: finally, supernumerary centrosomes promote chromosome mis-attachment and mis-segregation (Ganem et al., 2009; Silkworth et al., 2009), leading to chromosomal instability, a hallmark of cancer believed to drive tumor evolution (Targa and Rancati, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tetraploidy was shown to increase tolerance for genomic changes, leading to the rapid evolution of complex genomes.
source: For instance, tetraploidy was shown to increase tolerance for genomic changes, leading to the rapid evolution of complex genomes (Dewhurst et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Many tetraploid cells show increased chromosomal instability compared to diploid cells, even when no extra centrosomes are present.
source: and many tetraploid cells show increased chromosomal instability compared to diploid cells, even when no extra centrosomes are present (Kuznetsova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Polyploid cells were shown to be more resistant than their diploid counterparts to oxidative stress, genotoxic insult, irradiation, and certain chemotherapeutic drugs.
source: Additionally, polyploid cells were shown to be more resistant than their diploid counterparts to oxidative stress, genotoxic insult, irradiation, and certain chemotherapeutic drugs (Kuznetsova et al., 2015; Ianzini et al., 2009; Illidge et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In cancer patients, genome-doubling in early stage tumors was shown to correlate with poor relapse-free survival.
source: Lastly, in cancer patients, genome-doubling in early stage tumors was shown to correlate with poor relapse-free survival (Dewhurst et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In Barrett's esophagus, accumulation of 4N cells has been shown to occur as the tissue transitions to metaplasia.
source: In Barrett's esophagus, a pre-malignant condition that predisposes to esophageal cancer (Cameron et al., 1985; Hameeteman et al., 1989; Hvid-Jensen et al., 2011), accumulation of 4N cells has been shown to occur as the tissue transitions to metaplasia (Galipeau et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A study on centrosome status in Barrett's esophagus reported centrosome amplification prior to the transition to metaplasia.
source: A study on centrosome status in Barrett's esophagus reported centrosome amplification prior to the transition to metaplasia (Segat et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The frequency of supernumerary centrosomes decreased with progression to metaplasia and neoplasia in Barrett's esophagus.
source: but also noted that the frequency of supernumerary centrosomes decreased with progression to metaplasia and neoplasia (Segat et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Another study found an increase in centrosome amplification followed by a decrease during the progression from Barrett's Esophagus to adenocarcinoma.
source: Similarly, another study found an increase in centrosome amplification followed by a decrease during the progression from Barrett's Esophagus to adenocarcinoma (Lopes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Extra centrosomes can be present early in tumor development but subsequently be lost.
source: These results closely mirror the dynamics of evolution seen in our study and illustrate that extra centrosomes can be present early in tumor development (around the time when tetraploidy appears) but subsequently be lost.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature and comparison with the current study's findings.

claim: Clustering of extra centrosomes into a bipolar configuration can be influenced by a number of cell intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that clustering of extra centrosomes into a bipolar configuration can be influenced by a number of cell intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and such factors may be important for determining the fraction of cells that retain extra centrosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The nonessential motor protein KIFC1, the epithelial cell protein E-cadherin, spindle assembly checkpoint components, the chromosome passenger complex, the NDC80 complex, and the augmin complex have been shown to affect centrosome clustering efficiency.
source: Among cellular factors, the nonessential motor protein KIFC1 (also known as HSET), the epithelial cell protein E-cadherin, spindle assembly checkpoint components, the chromosome passenger complex, the NDC80 complex, and the augmin complex have been shown to affect (either positively or negatively) centrosome clustering efficiency (Kwon et al., 2008; Leber et al., 2010; Quintyne et al., 2005; Rhys et al., 2018; Sabino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Geometric constraints imposed by the environment have been shown to alter centrosome clustering.
source: Extracellular factors, such as geometric constraints imposed by the environment, have also been shown to alter centrosome clustering (Kwon et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.
